generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, creativity shows up across every subject as a way of meeting problems that have no routine answer. The questions that matter most in any field rarely come with a settled method, so progress depends on generating workable options and adapting them as constraints appear. Disciplines and employers alike name this habit, alongside adaptability and flexibility, among the attributes they most value.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students asked, in a careers task, to describe how creativity features in their future work.

Student A writes that professionals need to be creative thinkers and that creativity is valued everywhere. The claim is true but generic. It names creativity as a good thing without saying what problem it solves or how it would show up in practice, so it would read the same on any application in any field. This is creativity praised in the abstract.

Student B identifies a recurring problem that has no routine solution, then argues that this is where creativity earns its place: designing an unfamiliar approach and adapting it as conditions change. Creativity is tied to a concrete problem, linked to adaptability, and expressed as enterprise rather than as a personality trait. This is creativity appraised as an attribute.

Both students value creativity. Only Student B has treated it as an attribute: named, located in a real problem, and argued for in the terms a profession would recognise.
generatedProse.summary: Creativity earns its place among the graduate attributes that disciplines and employers prize because it generates workable options for problems that have no settled method, and because that habit transfers into professional practice. You can now appraise creativity as an attribute, relate it to adaptability and flexibility, and articulate how it shows up in your own field. The next lesson turns creativity onto how you regulate your own learning.

check.body: You are arguing that creativity matters in your field. Which move best shows creativity as a graduate attribute?

items.text: Naming a real problem with no routine solution and showing how a new option would address it.
Stating that professionals should be more creative.
Listing creativity among your strengths without an example.
Avoiding any problem that looks too difficult.

feedback.correct: That's right. Naming a problem with no routine solution and showing a new option argues creativity as an attribute.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that ties creativity to a concrete problem.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The attribute is argued by locating it in a real problem and a new option for it. Exhortation, bare lists and avoidance do not.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; name the cast directly in the prose (the pack supplies the whole body). The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
